front: What three fields define a tool in a Claude API request?
back: `name`, `description`, and `input_schema` — the last one is a JSON Schema for the arguments.

front: Your application has just executed the tool Claude asked for. What does it append to the conversation?
back: A `tool_result` content block; Claude continues the turn from that result.

front: What are the three accepted values for the `tool_choice` parameter?
back: `{"type": "auto"}` (the default), `{"type": "any"}`, and `{"type": "tool", "name": "X"}` for one named tool.

front: Which three keys carry the payload of a `tool_use` content block?
back: `id`, `name`, and `input`. The `id` is what the matching `tool_result` refers back to.

front: An agent picks the wrong one of two similar tools about half the time. What do you inspect before adding any new component to the system?
back: The two tool descriptions. Tool selection runs on descriptions, so they are the first suspect when routing goes wrong.

front: A tool description should answer four questions about the tool. What are they?
back: What it does, what input it accepts (formats, ID types, examples), when to use it over similar tools, and when not to use it.

front: A web-search agent's `analyze_content` and a document agent's `analyze_document` are confused nearly half the time. What is the fix the exam wants?
back: Rename the web-search tool to `extract_web_results` and rewrite its description to reference web search and URLs explicitly.
trap: Exam trap: a pre-routing classifier adds infrastructure that compensates for the ambiguous signal instead of correcting it.

front: A support agent has two tools with one-line descriptions, `get_customer` and `lookup_order`, whose ID formats look alike. Production logs show `get_customer` being called for order queries. What do you change?
back: Expand both descriptions with input formats, example queries, edge cases, and the boundary between the two tools.
trap: Exam trap: merging them into one `lookup_entity` tool ends the confusion by discarding the semantic precision that made two tools worth having.

front: Both tool descriptions already say what their tool does and the model still confuses them. Which single description element most directly separates the two?
back: The discriminating detail: accepted input formats with examples, when to choose this tool over the neighbouring one, and when not to use it at all.

front: Two candidate fixes for tool misrouting: few-shot examples showing correct selection, or rewritten tool descriptions. Which does the exam put first?
back: Rewritten descriptions. Examples and classifiers sit on top of the signal that is actually wrong.
trap: Exam trap: few-shot examples are a real technique elsewhere, and here they compensate for descriptions that never distinguished the tools.

front: Which flag does an MCP tool set on its result to signal that the call failed?
back: `isError: true`. The agent receives it and decides how to proceed.

front: What are the four tool-error categories the exam distinguishes?
back: Transient, validation, business, and permission.

front: Of the four error categories, which one should the agent retry unchanged?
back: Transient only, and ideally the tool or subagent already retried it internally before the agent ever saw it.

front: A tool rejects a malformed order ID. Which error category is that, and what is the agent supposed to do?
back: Validation. The call cannot succeed as sent: correct the input and call again.

front: A support agent's `process_refund` tool rejects a refund because the order falls outside the 30-day policy window, and the agent keeps calling it again with the same arguments. What should the tool have returned?
back: `retriable: false` plus a customer-friendly explanation of the policy, so the agent stops retrying and tells the customer why the refund was declined.
trap: Exam trap: a policy denial is a valid answer from a working tool; marking it transient with `isRetryable: true` spends retries on an outcome that can never change.

front: A `search_orders` query runs fine and matches nothing. What should the tool return?
back: A success with an empty result set — `isError` absent or false — so the agent can report 'no orders found' with confidence.

front: The orders database is unreachable and `search_orders` returns an empty list with no error flag. What does the agent then tell the customer?
back: That they have no orders — a false statement produced by masking an access failure as a valid empty result.
trap: Exam trap: the caller receives a well-formed answer, so nothing downstream can tell a masked outage apart from a genuine zero-match result.

front: Beyond a failure flag, what should a structured tool error carry so the coordinator can choose its next move?
back: An error category, a retryable flag, a description of what failed, any partial results, and suggested alternatives.

front: Where should a transient timeout be handled, and what reaches the coordinator?
back: Handled inside the tool or subagent with retry and backoff; the coordinator sees only what it alone can decide, along with partial results and what was attempted.

front: Of these three error designs, which is best and which is worst: a `retryable` boolean, raw error text the agent must interpret, or handling transient failures inside the tool?
back: Handling inside the tool is best; the `retryable` flag ranks second; forcing the agent to guess from error text is worst.
trap: Exam trap: the `retryable` flag is a genuine improvement over error text, which makes it an attractive pick even when internal handling is on offer.

front: A removal operation must always be previewed before it executes. What tool design makes skipping the preview impossible?
back: Two tools: `preview_remove_member` returns the impact details plus a single-use confirmation token, and `execute_remove_member` requires that token as a parameter.

front: Why does a `dry_run: boolean` parameter fail as a mandatory-preview mechanism?
back: The agent can call the tool with `dry_run: false` directly and never run the preview at all.
trap: Exam trap: the parameter makes a preview available, and the exam is asking for a design where the preview cannot be skipped.

front: A server-side timing heuristic, an orchestration-layer confirmation prompt, and a prompt instruction all try to force a preview before a destructive call. What does the two-tool design provide that none of the three does?
back: A structural guarantee: the token exists only after a preview call, so nothing depends on timing, extra infrastructure, or the model complying.

front: One subagent carries 18 tools and frequently calls the wrong one, while a peer with 5 role-scoped tools selects correctly. A teammate proposes writing more detailed descriptions for all 18. What does the exam prefer?
back: Cut each subagent's tool set to the 4-5 tools its role needs. Tool count is the root cause: every extra tool is one more candidate to tell apart on every turn.
trap: Exam trap: better descriptions do help, and applying them to 18 tools leaves the oversized decision space untouched.

front: What tool-count numbers does the official guide use for a well-scoped subagent versus the failing case?
back: 4-5 tools per subagent when scoped to a role; 18 in the case that misroutes.

front: A document-analysis agent given a generic `fetch_url` tool starts downloading search engine result pages. What is the sanctioned fix?
back: Replace it with a constrained `load_document` tool that validates the URL points at a document format, so the boundary is enforced at the interface.
trap: Exam trap: a prompt instruction is probabilistic and a search-engine domain blocklist is fragile; neither constrains the tool itself.

front: A synthesis agent needs single-fact confirmations constantly, and routing each one through the coordinator is slow. What is the sanctioned exception to strict role scoping?
back: A narrowly scoped cross-role tool: give it `verify_fact` for simple lookups, while complex research questions still route back through the coordinator.

front: Why is full `web_search` access the wrong way to cut the synthesis agent's fact-checking round-trips?
back: Agents given tools outside their specialization misuse them — the synthesis agent starts doing open-ended research instead of synthesizing.
trap: Exam trap: it does solve the latency complaint, by handing over a capability that belongs to the research role.

front: An extraction agent sometimes replies with prose instead of calling any extraction tool. What configuration guarantees a tool call?
back: `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}` — the model must call some tool and cannot return conversational text. With several extraction tools it still picks the best fit.
trap: Exam trap: `{"type": "auto"}` plus a 'you must use a tool' instruction still permits a text reply, because the instruction is probabilistic.

front: A pipeline must always extract document metadata before any enrichment tool runs. A prompt instruction saying so is followed about 90% of the time. How do you make the first step certain without blocking the rest of the workflow?
back: Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` on the first request, then relax to `"auto"` for the following turns.
trap: Exam trap: leaving the forced value on every turn guarantees the first step and stops the enrichment tools from ever being called.

front: What does `{"type": "auto"}` guarantee about the model's next response?
back: Nothing about tool use — the model may answer in plain text. That is the default and the right setting for most agentic loops.

front: What are MCP's three primitives, and what does each one provide?
back: Tools are actions Claude can call, resources are read-only data it can access, and prompts are pre-built templates.

front: An agent burns turn after turn calling `search_issues` with guessed queries just to discover what issues exist. Which MCP primitive removes that?
back: A resource. Expose an issue-summary catalog the agent can read for a map of the available data, then let it make targeted tool calls.

front: Why is adding a `list_everything` tool weaker than exposing the same catalog as an MCP resource?
back: A resource arrives as readable context on request; a tool costs an extra model call and only helps if the agent remembers to call it first.
trap: Exam trap: both surface the same data, and only the resource takes the discovery step out of the model's hands.

front: Why not paste the full issue database into the system prompt instead of exposing a resource?
back: Resources are requested on demand; a static dump is carried on every request and goes stale as the data changes.
trap: Exam trap: the dump does give the model its map, at the price of paying for it every turn and serving whatever was true at paste time.

front: What is the rule for choosing between an MCP tool and an MCP resource?
back: Resources for data the agent needs to read — catalogs, schemas, documentation hierarchies, fetched on demand. Tools for actions the agent needs to take.

front: Which MCP config file does a team commit to the repository, and which one stays on the individual developer's machine?
back: `.mcp.json` at the project root is the shared, version-controlled config; `~/.claude.json` in the user home holds personal auth and experimental servers.

front: A team shares one MCP server definition, but every developer authenticates with their own GitHub token. Where does the server definition go, and how does each token reach it?
back: Into `.mcp.json` with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` substitution and the variable documented in the README — Claude Code expands it from the environment at runtime.
trap: Exam trap: letting each developer add the server in user scope also works and leaves the team on inconsistent tooling; a committed placeholder token is the security-risk option.

front: For a standard Jira or GitHub integration, do you build a custom MCP server or adopt an existing one?
back: Adopt the existing community server. Custom servers are for unique, team-specific workflows that no existing server covers.
trap: Exam trap: building it yourself 'for control' reinvents a maintained standard integration and spends the custom-build effort in the wrong place.

front: A code-search MCP server offers semantic, index-backed search, and the agent keeps reaching for built-in Grep instead. What is the root cause?
back: The MCP tool's description does not make its advantage explicit, and tool selection runs on descriptions, so the familiar built-in wins.

front: Why is disabling built-in Grep the wrong way to push the agent toward a semantic code-search MCP tool?
back: It breaks legitimate content-search uses while leaving the under-specified MCP description exactly as it was.
trap: Exam trap: removing the alternative does change behavior; so does a blanket 'always prefer MCP tools' rule, which misroutes the cases where the built-in is right.

front: Built-in Grep and a semantic code-search MCP tool are both available. When is the built-in the right pick?
back: When the task is the plain content search Grep already handles. The MCP tool earns the call when it offers data or capability the built-in cannot provide.

front: Which hook fires before a tool executes, and which fires after?
back: `PreToolUse` before, to validate, block, or modify parameters; `PostToolUse` after, to transform output, log, or normalize.

front: Several third-party tools return dates in formats you cannot change at the source. What normalizes them?
back: A `PostToolUse` hook that intercepts the results and normalizes every output centrally.
trap: Exam trap: a `normalize_data` tool the agent calls after each retrieval adds a model call, and describing the formats in the system prompt leaves it to interpretation.

front: Bulk deletions affecting more than 50 records must always be escalated. Why does the exam pick a `PreToolUse` hook over a system-prompt rule?
back: Hooks are deterministic code that fires regardless of what the model decides; system-prompt instructions are probabilistic.

front: A support agent calls `get_customer` and `lookup_order` in separate sequential turns even when it needs both. What does the exam prefer?
back: Instruct the model in the prompt to bundle related tool requests into a single turn, since it can request several tools at once.

front: Why is a `get_customer_with_orders` composite tool the less-preferred fix for sequential tool calls?
back: It hides the composition inside a new tool when the model can already ask for both tools in one turn.
trap: Exam trap: the composite does remove the extra round trip, and the exam still prefers prompting for bundled requests.

front: Grep and Glob both locate things in a codebase. What does each one actually search?
back: Grep searches inside file contents for patterns; Glob matches file paths by name or extension pattern.

front: You need every file that references a deprecated `formatDate` function. Which built-in tool finds them?
back: Grep — the target is what is written inside the files, across the codebase.
trap: Exam trap: Glob `**/formatDate*` looks equivalent; Glob matches file paths, so it returns files named after the function and misses every caller.

front: A convention change has to reach every TypeScript test file. Which built-in tool enumerates them?
back: Glob with a pattern such as `**/*.test.tsx`, because the selection criterion is the file naming pattern.
trap: Exam trap: grepping for the word 'test' inside files matches unrelated files that mention testing and misses test files that never use the literal word.

front: On what does the Edit tool depend to locate the text it replaces?
back: A unique text match. When the anchor string occurs more than once, Edit cannot choose an occurrence and fails.

front: Edit fails because the anchor text is not unique in the file. What is the sanctioned fallback?
back: Read the full file, modify the content programmatically, then Write the updated version.

front: After an Edit fails on a non-unique anchor, a teammate retries with a shorter, more generic anchor string. What happens?
back: The odds get worse: a shorter string is likelier to occur in several places, so the same failure repeats.
trap: Exam trap: shortening reads like loosening a too-strict match, when the failure came from ambiguity that shortening increases.

front: Why is running `sed` through Bash the wrong way to force a replacement Edit could not make?
back: It bypasses the tool built for the job; the exam's sanctioned fallback is Read plus Write.
trap: Exam trap: `sed` does complete the replacement, and reaching for the shell when a structured tool exists is the documented anti-pattern.

front: You are dropped into an unfamiliar large repository and need to understand how one feature works end to end. Nobody has told you which files matter. What is the first move?
back: Grep for the entry points — the function definition or export — then Read what it finds and follow the imports outward, repeating until the picture holds.
trap: Exam trap: reading every file first to 'get full context' spends the context window on irrelevant files, which the exam treats as the anti-pattern.

front: A teammate proposes Globbing the whole tree and reading every match before running any content search. What is wrong with it?
back: Discovery should be driven by content search first, then targeted reads; enumerating and reading everything is bulk reading with an extra step.
trap: Exam trap: it uses the right tool for file enumeration and still reads everything before knowing what matters.

front: A rename of `calculateTax` must reach every caller. The function is wrapped by `utils/tax.ts` as `getTax` and re-exported from `index.ts`. Grepping for `calculateTax` returns a short list of call sites. What step is missing?
back: Collect every exported name first — the original plus each wrapper or re-export alias — then Grep for each name to find the rest of the call sites.

front: Which category of work is Bash the right built-in tool for?
back: Running shell commands: git, npm, tests, builds. Reading, searching, and editing files each have a dedicated tool.

front: Which tool errors are worth retrying, and which are guaranteed to fail the same way again?
back: Transient errors such as timeouts and network faults retry with backoff. Validation, permission, and business-rule errors return immediately with detail.
trap: Exam trap: uniform backoff across every failure burns attempts on a policy denial that no number of retries can change.

front: A search tool returns zero matches. A second call times out. Which of the two is an error?
back: Only the timeout. Zero matches is a successful query with an empty result set, so `isError` stays absent or false.
trap: Exam trap: flagging zero matches as an error makes the agent retry a query that worked; returning an empty list for a failed query makes it report no data.

front: Why is merging two confusable tools into a single `lookup_entity` tool the wrong repair?
back: It discards the semantic precision that lets the model tell the two cases apart, while the ambiguity itself lives in the descriptions.
trap: Exam trap: consolidation presents as simplification and removes the very distinction the agent was failing to make.
